title: Not yet
hook: Ananda was still unawakened when the Buddha died, and wept

segments.voice: Yesterday, water from the well, and your line: I asked for water. Whose kindness did you take gladly? Today, a long night for Ananda, and what he still hadn't reached. Day seven hundred thirty-six.

Night, in a grove of sal trees at Kusinara. The Buddha is dying. Around him are monks of every kind: some, the texts say, fully free, and some still on the way. Ananda is among the second group. He has been at the teacher's side for many years, and kept what he heard. And he is not yet awakened. Earlier on this path we watched him slip away to weep in a doorway, and the Buddha call him back. Today, let's stay with those two words that sit under the whole scene: not yet.
screen: `A GROVE AT KUSINARA.` → `SOME FREE, SOME ON THE WAY.` → `NOT YET.`

segments.voice: First, the start, long before. In the Samyutta Nikaya, Ananda remembers that when he was newly ordained, a monk named Punna taught him, and hearing it, he broke through to the teaching. So Ananda had entered the path early. He wasn't a beginner on this night. He was a learner. Second, the learner at the end. The Pali word is sekha: one still in training, on the path but not at its end. In the doorway, Ananda says it of himself, in paraphrase: I'm still a learner, with work left to do, and my teacher, who was so kind to me, is passing away. And the Buddha doesn't call that failure. He tells Ananda he has served him well, and says: keep at it, and you'll soon be free. Soon. Not now. Third, the night itself. When the Buddha passes, the discourse says some monks weep and some bear it calmly: everything made comes apart. Ananda speaks a verse about the shock of that moment. And then, the text says, Anuruddha, one of the monks already free, and Ananda spent the rest of that night together, talking about the teaching. The finished one and the unfinished one, side by side until morning. Nobody sent the learner away. Fourth, what not yet means. It isn't never. In the texts, the learner is already on the path and counted among the noble disciples. Ananda had kept what he heard, served his teacher faithfully, and still wasn't done, and the story treats that as a place to stand rather than a verdict. Tomorrow we'll see how not yet ended.
screen: `A START, LONG BEFORE.` · `STILL A LEARNER AT THE END.` · `A NIGHT OF TALK WITH ANURUDDHA.` · `NOT YET ISN'T NEVER.` · then, large: `NOT YET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be patient with yourself. Settle, and breathe. Name one thing in your life that's still not finished. A habit you're still working on. A skill. A grief. Something you thought you'd have sorted by now. Say it plainly to yourself, and then add two words: not yet. Notice what changes when you say not yet instead of never. Then, the way the Buddha did for Ananda, name one thing you have already done well. Hold both. Rest with the breath until the end. The bell holds the time.
Not yet. When the Buddha died, Ananda was still a learner, on the path and not at its end, and he wept; the Buddha's word for him was soon. Today's word.
Your line: not yet. Today, when you catch yourself saying I'll never get this, change it, out loud if you can, to not yet. Day seven hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: In Theravada teaching, a sekha or learner is a disciple who has entered the path but not completed it, and Ananda's story is told to encourage practitioners who are still on the way.

original.note: Pali: a learner, one in training; a disciple who has entered the path but not finished it.

trapdoor: what you thought: not yet means you're failing.
what it means: Ananda entered the path early and was still a learner at the end; the Buddha's word for him was soon.
what a scholar hears: sekha is a technical term for a noble disciple still in training, and the texts place Ananda there on the night of the Buddha's death.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), Ananda as learner; the passing; Anuruddha and Ananda through the night

notes: All material paraphrased. Year two, day 550 told the doorway scene and the Buddha's praise in detail; this day takes the learner (sekha) angle and the night after the passing instead. Confirm the overlap is acceptable.
Confirm SN 22.83: Ananda says Punna Mantaniputta helped him when newly ordained and that on hearing his teaching he 'broke through to the Dhamma' (stream-entry).

Confirm DN 16: Ananda's 'I am still a learner (sekha) with work to do' (5.13); the Buddha's 'you will soon be free of the taints' (5.14); Ananda's verse at the moment of passing (6.10); the monks not free of passion weeping and those free bearing it mindfully; Anuruddha and Ananda spending the rest of the night in Dhamma talk (6.11-12).
howItsDone: 'often told to encourage practitioners' is general; confirm or soften.
Editor: cut 'every word, every day', changed 'young' to 'early' and the screen 'years before' to 'long before' (the text says newly ordained, no age or count).
